newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco's image has improved, says royal aide.
newsitem.headline: Morocco's image has improved, says royal aide.

text.p: Morocco's image abroad has improved in recent years, mirroring political and economic reforms, but social issues are still hampering competitiveness, a top official said on Friday.
King Hassan's adviser for economic affairs, Andre Azoulay, was addressing a three-day scientific meeting on "The place of Morocco in the World" which ended on Friday night.
"Five years ago, Morocco suffered from an image crisis ... everybody was talking of crisis, (economic) problems and difficulties," Azoulay said.
But he said this "negative image" had changed due to government efforts in the political and economic sectors.

Azoulay has just returned from accompanying Crown Prince Sidi Mohammed on an official visit to the United States where the prince met President Bill Clinton in Washington and the business community in New York.

"During my visit to the United States, I found that Morocco's image was restored and reflects the picture of an emerging market with a growing economy...But this is not sufficient to face the next century challenges...We have to work hard together to build our future," Azoulay said.

Morocco, which ended a structural adjustment in 1992, embarked on financial and monetary reforms in 1993. It also announced regional and political reforms that included elections for a new bicameral parliament in 1997.
The political change was backed by the main opposition parties for the first time since the independence in 1956.
"Morocco has no more a problem of image, but I do not think that we can say everything is fine and our (social) problems were solved and we have no difficulties," Azoulay said.
"We have to carry on our (economic and political) reforms and move forward," he added.
The three-day meeting discussed issues including the competitiveness of Moroccan firms, budget deficits, inflation, unemployment, social disparities and illiteracy.
A Moroccan economist told the meeting that faster growth was needed to improve the living standards of Morocco's 27 million people and create a healthy climate for competition.

"But the country's social disparities and high illiteracy remain a serious obstacle to a balanced development between urban and rural areas," Driss Ben Ali, a prominent economist and university professor, said.
Illiteracy is estimated at more than 55 percent of the population.
The government is seeking at least 7.0 to 8.0 percent growth in future in GDP to improve living standards and eradicate illteracy, officials said.
"If we maintain a positive growth in the coming decade, the GDP could reach at least $3,000 per head from the present $1,200," a government official said.
Growth in GDP is expected to top 10 percent this year after a figure of minus 7.6 percent in 1995 due to a severe drought.
